rv.q: In a category all its own is Christopher Nightingale's Tony-winning score, which couples original composition with a panoply of carols whose arrangements moisten the eye before a word has even been spoken.
From the mince pies and satsumas given out as you enter, to the impossibly jaunty cast and falling snow, this is a Christmas production that still warms you to your core.
It’s a bundle of laughs from start to finish – and in classic Christmas Carol tradition, there’s some heart-warming moments at the end.
As the ensemble deliver a final carol, with bells, the feelgood factor has been well and truly earned.
A CHRISTMAS CAROL is charm itself, runs 2 hours and 20 mins (including interval), and continues until 9th January 2027.

Jack Thorne's script is pitched so an eight-year-old can follow it, then slips in things the parents will recognise, and the children only will later: deep regret, the lifelong impact of bad parenting, love postponed until it has gone, and how quickly a life folds itself away.
This production is missing hues and shadows of previous ones.
Thorne and Warchus do a beautiful job of bringing a crotchety London crowd together, with much Christmas cheer for adults and children alike, and a hot mince pie to boot.
It'll leave you feeling warm, inspired and most of all, filled with hope.
The Old Vic's unstoppable annual show remains magical as ever
There's no more welcome theatrical perennial these days than Jack Thorne's take on A Christmas Carol at the Old Vic
It is the greatest Christmas story ever told.
Ten years on, this production still has plenty of festive magic to share.
Matthew Warchus's richly atmospheric production has lost none of its magic.

cn.t: The Old Vic's A Christmas Carol, now in its 10th season, remains a beloved festive institution. Critics largely praise its emotional power and Jack Thorne's adaptation, though a few find the familiar formula showing its age.
